entries.title: Sun
entries.summary: The star at the centre of the Solar System: an ordinary G-type main-sequence star, and the calibration point for every other star.
body: Everything we know about other stars is measured against the Sun. It is the only star whose surface we can resolve in fine detail, whose interior we can probe with **helioseismology** (sound waves ringing through it), and whose neutrinos we catch directly.
Its energy comes from nuclear fusion in the core, where hydrogen is turned into helium. Its light takes about **8 minutes 19 seconds** to cross the 1 au to Earth.

facts.label: Effective temperature
facts.method: Stefan–Boltzmann law applied to the measured luminosity and photospheric radius

facts.label: Photospheric radius
facts.method: Solar limb measurements referred to the photosphere (where the gas becomes opaque); the IAU nominal radius, 695,700 km, is this value rounded

facts.label: Luminosity
facts.method: Total solar irradiance measured from space (1361 W/m², averaged over solar cycle 23) over a sphere 1 au in radius

facts.label: Gravitational parameter GM
facts.method: Fitted to planetary and spacecraft ranging (JPL DE440)

facts.label: Age
facts.method: Radiometric dating of the oldest solids in meteorites, assumed to have formed with the Sun

howWeKnow.claim: The Sun's size, temperature and power output are **measured**: satellites record its total irradiance, and observations of its limb give its radius.
howWeKnow.method: Space radiometry and solar limb observations

howWeKnow.claim: Its age is **inferred**, not measured: the oldest meteorite grains are dated radiometrically, and the Sun is assumed to have formed with them.

entries.title: Earth
entries.summary: Our home world, the third planet from the Sun and the only place known to host life.
body: Earth is the yardstick for every rocky planet in the Codex: when an exoplanet's radius is given as **0.92 Earth radii**, this is the planet being compared.

Its shape is measured to about ten centimetres by satellite geodesy. Its mass enters through **GM**, the product of the gravitational constant and the mass, which spacecraft tracking pins down far better than either factor alone.

In Known Sky, Earth's colours come from NASA's Blue Marble imagery and its relief from ETOPO1 elevation data. Detail finer than the data is **generated**: seeded noise that looks plausible but is invented.

facts.label: Equatorial radius
facts.method: Satellite geodesy (IAU WGCCRE 2015 report)

facts.label: Polar radius
facts.method: Satellite geodesy (IAU WGCCRE 2015 report)

facts.label: Gravitational parameter GM
facts.method: Fitted to lunar laser ranging and spacecraft tracking (JPL DE440)

facts.label: Surface colour
facts.method: Cloud-free MODIS satellite mosaic

facts.label: Elevation grid
facts.method: Global relief model from satellite altimetry and ship surveys

facts.label: Terrain finer than the grid
facts.method: Seeded noise added below the resolution of the elevation data

facts.label: Age
facts.method: Radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial and lunar rocks

howWeKnow.claim: Earth's size and shape are **measured**: satellite laser ranging and altimetry tie the surface to the planet's centre of mass.
Its age is **inferred**: no rock survives from Earth's formation, so it is dated through meteorites that formed at the same time.
Surface detail below the 1 arc-minute data grid is **generated** for the game.

entries.title: Moon
entries.summary: Earth's only natural satellite, and the only other world people have walked on.
body: The Moon always shows Earth the same face: it is **tidally locked**, turning once on its axis for every orbit.

Retroreflectors left by Apollo astronauts and Lunokhod rovers still return laser pulses fired from Earth. Timing those echoes measures the Earth–Moon distance to centimetres, and shows the Moon **slowly drifting away**.
How the Moon formed is not observed but inferred: the leading explanation is a giant impact between the young Earth and a Mars-sized body.

facts.label: Mean radius
facts.method: Laser altimetry and imaging (IAU WGCCRE 2015 report)

facts.label: Gravitational parameter GM
facts.method: Lunar laser ranging and spacecraft tracking (JPL DE440)

facts.label: Semi-major axis of orbit
facts.method: Orbit determination

facts.label: Sidereal orbital period
facts.method: Orbit determination

facts.label: Recession from Earth
facts.method: Lunar laser ranging to the Apollo retroreflectors

facts.label: Surface elevation
facts.method: Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter

howWeKnow.claim: The distance to the Moon is **measured** by timing laser pulses reflected from mirrors placed on its surface.
The Moon most likely formed from debris after a **giant impact** on the early Earth.
howWeKnow.method: Impact simulations matched to the Earth–Moon angular momentum and the Moon's small iron core

entries.title: Proxima Centauri
entries.summary: The nearest star to the Sun: a small, cool red dwarf about 4.2 light-years away, with at least one planet.
body: Proxima Centauri is far too faint to see without a telescope, even though no star is closer. It is a **red dwarf**, the most common kind of star in the Galaxy.
Its distance comes from **parallax**: as Earth orbits the Sun, Proxima appears to shift against far more distant stars, and the size of that shift gives the distance directly.

facts.label: Parallax
facts.method: Gaia space astrometry (Data Release 3)

facts.label: Distance
facts.method: Inverse of the parallax

facts.label: First planet found
facts.method: Radial velocity (the star's wobble)

howWeKnow.claim: Proxima's distance is **measured** by parallax, using geometry alone.

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1
entries.summary: An ultracool red dwarf about 40 light-years away, orbited by seven Earth-sized planets.
body: TRAPPIST-1 is only slightly larger than Jupiter and has less than a tenth of the Sun's mass. It is so dim that all seven of its planets orbit closer to it than Mercury does to the Sun.
All seven planets **transit**: they pass in front of the star as seen from Earth. Their tug on one another shifts the timing of those transits, and that is how their masses were weighed.

facts.label: Luminosity
facts.method: Bolometric flux and distance (Ducrot et al. 2020, as adopted by Agol et al.)

facts.label: Mass
facts.method: Empirical relation between near-infrared brightness and mass for M dwarfs (Mann et al. 2019), as adopted by Agol et al.

facts.label: Radius
facts.method: Stellar density from the planets' transits, combined with the inferred mass

facts.label: Effective temperature
facts.method: Stefan–Boltzmann law from the luminosity and the inferred radius

facts.label: Spectral type
facts.method: Optical and near-infrared spectroscopy

facts.label: Age
facts.method: Kinematics, rotation, activity and metallicity indicators

howWeKnow.claim: The star's **luminosity** is measured: its total brightness across all wavelengths, scaled by its distance.
Its mass is **inferred** from its brightness, using a relation calibrated on M dwarfs in binary systems.
Its radius and temperature are **inferred** too: the transits give the star's density, the inferred mass turns that into a radius, and the luminosity and radius give the temperature.
howWeKnow.method: Transit photometry and the Stefan–Boltzmann law

entries.title: TRAPPIST-1 e
entries.summary: A rocky planet slightly smaller than Earth, in the zone around TRAPPIST-1 where liquid water could be stable on the surface.
body: TRAPPIST-1 e receives about **65%** of the starlight Earth gets from the Sun, which places it in its star's habitable zone. Whether it actually has water, or any atmosphere at all, is not yet known.
Its radius comes from how much starlight it blocks in transit, and its mass from transit-timing variations. Together they give a density close to Earth's, consistent with a rocky planet.
**JWST** has observed its transits. The data rule out a cloudy hydrogen-dominated atmosphere, but cannot yet tell whether a thinner, Earth-like one exists.
No one has seen its surface. The landscape you fly over in Known Sky is **generated** from the inferred rocky composition.

facts.label: Radius
facts.method: Transit photometry (Spitzer, K2 and ground-based telescopes)

facts.label: Mass
facts.method: Transit-timing variations (photodynamical fit)

facts.label: Density
facts.method: Derived from the mass and radius

facts.label: Orbital period
facts.method: Transit timing

facts.label: Starlight received (Earth = 1)
facts.method: Computed from the star's luminosity and the planet's orbit

facts.label: Equilibrium temperature
facts.method: Computed for zero albedo and full heat redistribution; the real surface temperature depends on an unknown atmosphere

facts.label: Hydrogen-rich atmosphere
facts.method: JWST NIRSpec transmission spectroscopy of four transits

facts.label: Surface terrain
facts.method: Seeded terrain chosen from the inferred rocky composition

howWeKnow.claim: Radius and mass are **measured**: the radius from transit depths, the mass from transit-timing variations caused by the other planets.
A thick hydrogen atmosphere is **ruled out**; whether a thin secondary atmosphere exists is still open.
The surface shown in the game is **invented** within those constraints.

entries.title: Parallax
entries.summary: How astronomers measure the distance to a star without assuming anything about the star: geometry alone.
body: Hold up a finger and close each eye in turn: the finger jumps against the background. Nearby stars do the same as Earth moves around the Sun, but the shift is tiny.

A star whose apparent position swings by one arcsecond either side of its average is one **parsec** away, about 3.26 light-years. Even Proxima Centauri, the nearest star, shifts by less than an arcsecond.
The **Hipparcos** and **Gaia** satellites measured parallaxes from space, free of the blurring atmosphere. Many star distances in Known Sky's catalogue come from them.

facts.label: Parallax of Proxima Centauri
facts.method: Gaia space astrometry (Data Release 3)

facts.label: Stars in the new Hipparcos reduction
facts.method: Space astrometry, 1989–1993

facts.label: Distance of Proxima Centauri
facts.method: One over the parallax in arcseconds gives the distance in parsecs (1.302); one parsec is about 3.26 light-years

howWeKnow.claim: Parallax needs no assumptions about the star itself: only the size of Earth's orbit and a precise angle.
The first stellar parallax was measured by Friedrich Bessel in 1838, for the star 61 Cygni.

entries.title: The hyperspeed drive
entries.summary: The one thing in Known Sky that is pure fiction.
body: The universe in Known Sky is built from real measurements. The drive that carries you between stars is not: no known physics allows travel faster than light.
It is there because the alternative is waiting more than four years to reach even the nearest star. Everything you find when you arrive is labelled for what it is.

facts.label: Drive speed
facts.method: Game mechanic, chosen for playability rather than physics

facts.label: Distance to the nearest star
facts.method: Gaia parallax of Proxima Centauri: light needs more than four years to cover it
